en: I take refuge in the state of Śrī Rāma, which shines as the very nature of the glory of liberation (kaivalya), which is the imperishable light,
and which is entirely free from all counter-correlates (pratiyogin).

Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Worshipful Ones. With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise you and attain the lifespan ordained by the Gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unharmed, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Oṃ. The Rahasya, the Ramatapata, the Vāsudeva, the Mudgala, the Śāṇḍilya, the Paiṅgala, the Bhikṣu, the Mahacchārīraka, and the Śikhā. 1.
Then Sanaka and other eminent yogis, as well as other sages and devotees of Viṣṇu such as Prahlāda, spoke to Hanumān.
O mighty-armed son of Vāyu, what is the essential truth of those who discourse on Brahman,
as found in the eighteen Purāṇas and also in the eighteen Smṛtis?

"O one of great power, tell me: among these— the four Vedas, the Śāstras, the sciences, the spiritual self-knowledge, all the names of Viṣṇu, and the deities Vighna, Sūrya, Īśa, and Śakti— which is the true reality?"
Hanumān said:
O lords of yogis, and likewise you sages who are devotees of Viṣṇu,
listen to my words which destroy the bonds of worldly existence.
In all these very things, the reality is the liberating Brahman;
Rāma alone is the supreme Brahman, the reality, Śrī Rāma is the liberating Brahman.
Those lords of yogis and sages, devotees of Viṣṇu, were addressed by the son of Vāyu and asked Hanumān: "Tell us of the limbs of Rāma.
Hanumān said: [One should worship] the son of Vāyu, Vighneśa, Vāṇī, and Durgā.
Kṣetrapālaka, Sūrya, Candra, Nārāyaṇa, Nārasiṃha,
Vāyudeva, Vārāha, and all those of equal measure; Sīta, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, Bharata, Vibhīṣaṇa, Sugrīva, and Aṅgada.
"You should know that Jāmbavān is the *praṇava* and these others are the limbs (*aṅga*) of Rāma;
without those limbs, Rāma becomes an obstacle.
Then, addressed again by the son of the Wind, they questioned Hanumān.

"O Āñjaneya of great strength, how can there be an entitlement to the *praṇava* for Brahmins who are householders? He replied, "Śrī Rāma himself has said this: 'Only those who possess the entitlement to the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*) shall have the entitlement to the *praṇava*, and no others.'"

I shall be the bringer of auspiciousness for one who, having meditated upon the *praṇava* together with the syllables *a*, *u*, *m*, and the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), recites the *rāma-mantra*. [This applies] to that *praṇava*'s *a*-syllable,
its *u*-syllable, its *m*-syllable, and its half-measure.

Having daily recited the seer, the meter, the deity, the arrangement of their respective syllables and letters, and the qualities of the vowels, the Vedas, and the fires, and having chanted the Praṇava mantra twice as many times,
he who thereafter chants the Rāma-mantra becomes Rāma himself.
Therefore, it was said by Rāma that the Praṇava is the limb (aṅga) of Rāma.
Vibhīṣaṇa said:
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground before Rāma, the slayer of Paulastya, who was seated upon the lion-throne, the descendant of Pulastya spoke these words.
O mighty-armed Raghunātha, you have spoken only of accessibility; now the accessibility of the limbs must also be explained. (8)

Śrī Rāma said: Now, regarding the five offenses— the killer of a father, the killer of a mother, the killer of a Brahmin, the slayer of a guru, and the killer of ten million people— he who, having committed many sins,
chants my ninety-six crore names is liberated from those sins.
"He is liberated. Will he not himself become the very nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss?
Vibhīṣaṇa spoke again: "If he is incapable even of that, what does he do?
He said to him: "O son of Kaikasī, if one is incapable of performing the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa),"
Whoever [recites] my Great Upaniṣad, my Gītā, my Thousand Names, my Universal Form, my One Hundred and Eight [Names], the Rāma-śatābhidhāna,
the King of Hymns spoken by Nārada, and the hymn consisting of the King of Mantras proclaimed by Hanumān—
And for one who constantly praises me with mantras such as the "Sītā-stava" and the "Rāma-ṣaḍakṣarī," would they not become equal to me? Would they not indeed become so?
Thus ends the first chapter. || 1 ||
The sages, Sanaka and others, questioned Hanumān:
"O mighty son of Añjanā, tell us the collection of mantras belonging to Rāmacandra, the Tārakabrahman."
Hanumān said:
The bed of Viṣṇu situated in the fire is adorned with the crescent moon.
The single-syllable mantra is proclaimed as the king of mantras, a celestial tree. (1)

For the mantra whose self is Fire (the *agni-mantra*), Brahmā is the sage, the Gāyatrī is the meter, and Rāma is the deity; one should form its limbs with [the syllables] joined by a long *ardhendu* (half-moon). || 2 ||
By means of the seed-syllable and its powers, one should employ it for the desired purpose upon a lotus seat on a mandāra altar-platform on the bank of the Sarayū river.
Dark-complexioned, seated in the virāsana posture, adorned with the mudrā of knowledge,
his hand resting upon his left thigh, and accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
Beholding himself within himself as one of immeasurable splendor,
resembling pure crystal, he remained solitary out of a longing for liberation.
Meditating upon the Supreme Self, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
[the fires are] Vahni, Nārāyaṇa, the Nāḍīs, Jāṭhara, and Kevala.
Therefore, this two-syllabled king of mantras bestows all desired objects;
its seer and other [limbs] are those stated for the one-syllabled mantra, and the six-limbed ritual is performed with the first syllable.
The sixfold King of Mantras consists of the syllables *tāra*, *māyā*, *ramā*, *anaṅga*, *vāk*, and one's own seed-syllable; it is three-syllabled and bestows all desired fruits. || 8 ||
The two-syllable [mantra] ends with Candrabhadra, and the four-syllable [mantra] is of two kinds;
the seers and other details for these two should be understood by the wise as before. (9)

The two *ram* sounds, together with their bases, are situated in the wind; this five-syllabled mantra is held to have Viśvāmitra as its seer (*ṛṣi*), the *paṅkti* meter, and [the aforementioned] deity. (10)
One should place the mantra sequentially— Rāmabhadra, Bīja, Śakti, and the first letter—
at the center of the eyebrows, the heart, the navel, the thighs, and the feet.
One should know the six-limbed [protection] as before, and the weapon-mantra with the syllables of the mantra;
in the center, at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree in a grove, upon a seat of flowers and creepers.
Lakṣmaṇa, with the corner of his eye,
aimed an arrow at the Lord as he watched Jānakī while she was fanning him.
With his head radiant with a mass of matted locks, dark-complexioned, and surrounded by hosts of sages, he was seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot while Lakṣmaṇa held a parasol over him. || 14 ||
Having thus obtained the peaceful mantra of the crusher of Asura’s pride, along with Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa,
one who desires victory should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Svakāma, Śakti, Vāg, Lakṣmī, and Stava are the first five syllables;
the six-syllabled mantra is thus sixfold and bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. || 16 ||
Preceded by each of the fifty syllables of the Mātṛkā-mantra,
[the mantra] may be of many kinds, beginning with Lakṣmī, Vāk, Manmatha, and Tārā.
The mantra situated within each of the single seed-syllables of Śrī, Māyā, and Manmatha shall consist of either four or six syllables; it is indeed the bestower of all desires. (18)
This six-syllable mantra is said to have one hundred and twenty-eight variations, ending either with *svāhā*, *huṃ phaṭ*, or *namaḥ*. (19)
Brahmā, Sammohana, Śakti, Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
Agastya, and Śiva— these are declared to be the sages in this sequence.
The meter is known as Gāyatrī, and the deity is Śrī Rāma;
alternatively, for the Kāmabīja and others, Viśvāmitra is the sage and Manu is the deity. (21)
The meter is Gāyatrī belonging to the goddess Chanda and others; Rāmabhadra is its deity.
One should assign the six syllables in sequence, with the seed-syllable (bīja) and power-syllable (śakti) as before.

One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), between the eyebrows, at the heart, the navel, the thighs, and the feet, using either the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels or the individual letters of the mantra.
[I bow to] Rāghava, whose lovely luster is like that of a dark rain cloud, who sits perpetually in the heroic posture (vīrāsana),
who holds in one lotus-hand the mudrā consisting of primordial wisdom while the other rests upon his knee,
and beside whom stands Sītā, holding a lotus in her hand and resembling a flash of lightning.
I worship Him who gazes [upon me], His limbs radiant with various ornaments such as a crown and armlets. || 24 ||

Śrīrāma, ending with candrabhadra, followed by the nasal *ṅ*, and joined with *nati* (namas), is the seven-syllabled king of mantras, which bestows the fruits of all desires; it exists in two forms. || 25 ||

That [mantra] as well, when accompanied by Tāra and others, is considered to be of two kinds and consists of eight syllables: Tāra, Rāma, the word in the dative case, the breast, the weapon, and she who lies upon the bed of fire (Śrī). // 26 //
This supreme eight-syllabled mantra has the same seer (ṛṣi) and other attributes as the six-syllabled one.
Furthermore, for this eight-syllabled mantra, Rāma alone is traditionally remembered as the seer.
The deity of this [mantra] "gāyatraṃ chandaḥ" is Rāma himself;
the syllable Om (tāra), the pair of Śrī-bījas, and so forth are considered its seed-syllables (bīja), power (śakti), and other attributes. || 28 ||

Then the wise practitioner should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the very syllables of the mantra; he should utter the Tāra (Oṃ), the pair of Śrī-bījas (Śrīṃ Śrīṃ), and "Rāmāya Namaḥ. (29)
One should utter the seed-syllable *glauṃ moṃ*, then *māyā* (hrīṃ), and again *hṛdrāmāya* (namaḥ).
This is the mantra of Śivomārāma; it consists of eight syllables and bestows wealth.
The sage is declared to be Sadāśiva; the Gāyatrī is said to be the metre;
and Śivomārāmacandra is proclaimed here as the deity. (31)
With long illusory powers joined with the five syllables beginning with *Tāra*,
we worship the supreme Rāma— the three-eyed one, who bears the crescent moon and the trident,
whose entire body is smeared with ashes, and who wears his hair in a matted lock.
One should meditate upon her who is delightful to Rāma, the pinnacle of beauty, adorned with the moon as her crest-ornament, holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, and possessing three eyes.
Meditating thus, intent upon reciting the mantra one million times and performing libations,
he should offer oblations with bilva leaves, fruits, flowers, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and lotuses.
Treasures and supernatural powers desired even by the gods come to him of their own accord;
furthermore, O Raghavas, there is the eight-syllabled mantra of the Brahman-Gāyatrī.
The seers and so forth are to be known as my Śrī-bīja, which possesses power;
its application is for the sake of pleasing that [deity], and the assignment of the limbs is performed by means of the mantra-syllables. (36)
Rāma, ever resplendent with armlets, shoulder-ornaments, and bracelets set with gems, and shining with a parasol resembling ten million full moons,
was seated in the center of a great pavilion adorned with sixteen thousand golden pillars.
I worship the dark-complexioned Rāma, the Lord of Gods, surrounded by Bharata and the others. 37.

What is the use of many mantras that yield perishable fruits, which are achieved through great exertion, which result in nothing more than a mere expansion of greed, and which bring about the sufferings of saṃsāra?
Even though he is alone, he bestows the fruit of all mantras, being free from defects such as greed.
"Śrī Rāma is my refuge"—this eight-syllabled mantra should be constantly recited. (38)
Thus, the eight-syllable mantra has been correctly proclaimed in seven ways;
the seven-syllable Rāma-mantra is joined with the *tāra* at both the beginning and the end. (39)
The king of mantras shall consist of nine syllables; the remainder should be arranged as in the six-syllable mantra.
One should place "Jānakīvallabha" ending in the suffix -ṅe, followed by "vahnerjāyā" (svāhā) and "hum" and so forth.
This ten-syllabled mantra bestows the fruits of all desired objects.
For this ten-syllabled mantra, Vasiṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi) and Virāṭ is the meter (chandas). || 41 ||
Its meter is Anuṣṭubh, its presiding deity is Rāma who took Sītā’s hand in marriage;
the first syllable is the seed-syllable (bīja), the letter Ṭha is the power (śakti), and the performance of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) is considered to be with the Kāma-mantra. || 42 ||
One should place the ten syllables of the mantra upon the head, forehead, between the eyebrows, the palate, the ears, the heart, as well as the navel, thighs, knees, and feet. (43)
In the city of Ayodhyā, which was variegated with jewels, within a golden pavilion where canopies were tied with mandāra flowers and adorned with arched gateways; || 44 ||
Rāghava was seated upon a lion-throne atop the Puṣpaka chariot,
surrounded by Rākṣasas, monkeys, and auspicious gods traveling in divine vehicles.
He was being praised by sages who bowed low and attended upon him;
his left side was adorned by Sītā, and he was served by Lakṣmaṇa.
Meditating thus upon the dark-complexioned one with a serene face, adorned with all ornaments, one should recite the mantra for one hundred thousand syllables with undistracted mind. (47)

The mantra "rāmaṃ ṅentaṃ dhanuṣpāṇaye" ending with the nasal (ṅ), with the word "antah" [as the seed-syllable], and "vahnisundarī" [svāhā] at the end, constitutes this ten-syllabled mantra; its sage is said to be Brahmā and its meter Virāṭ. || 48 ||
The meter is said to be the deity, and Rāma, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas;
one should perform the remainder as before and visualize him bearing the bow and arrow. (49)
The ten-syllable king of mantras is sixfold, consisting of the syllables *tāra*, *māyā*, *ramā*, *anaṅga*, *vāk*, and its own seed-syllable; this mantra consists of eleven syllables.
The remaining procedures, such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), should be understood by the wise to be like those for the six-syllable mantra.
For the twelve-syllable mantra, Śrī Rāma is said to be the seer (*ṛṣi*). (51)
The Jagatī meter is said [to be the meter], and Śrī Rāma is considered the deity;
the Praṇava is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja), "klīṃ" is the power (śakti), and "hrīṃ" is the pin (kīlaka). || 52 ||
Having performed the placement of the limbs with the mantra, one should perform the remaining rites as before;
having uttered the *tāra* (Om), the *māyā* (Hrīṃ), and also the words "Bharatāgraja" (the elder brother of Bharata).
"Rāmaṃ klīṃ" ending with the fire-born wife (svāhā)—this is the twelve-syllabled mantra.
"Oṃ hṛdbhagavate rāmacandrabhadrau" followed by the dative suffix (ṅe). (54)
Its deity is Arka (the Sun), and it is of two kinds; its seer, meditation, and so forth are as before.
The meter is indeed Jagatī, and the arrangement of the limbs is according to the number of syllables in the mantra. (55)
Having uttered the word "Śrīrāma," and thereafter "Jayarāma," the wise one should utter the two words "Jaya" twice; this is the king of mantras, "Rāma. (56)
The mantra consists of thirteen syllables; its seer and other [limbs] are as before, and it grants all desires.
The ritual application (*aṅga*) is performed by repeating the two words twice, and the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as in the ten-syllable mantra.
That [mantra] of fourteen syllables, accompanied by Tārā and the others, should be uttered as thirteen syllables, and after that, one should join it with the word "Rāma. (58)
This fifteen-syllable mantra is indeed a wish-fulfilling tree for those who recite it: "Namas ca sītāpataye rāmāya" followed by "hana" twice. (59)
Then, the sixteen-syllable mantra ending with the armor (*kavaca*) and weapons (*astra*) is proclaimed; its seer is Agastya, its meter is Bṛhatī, and its deity is he [Śiva] himself. (60)
The seed-syllable is *rāṃ*, the power (*śakti*) and the weapon (*astra*) are likewise [assigned], and *huṃ* is declared to be the bolt (*kīlaka*).
One should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*) in sequence using all the syllables—two, five, three, and four respectively.
That mantra, accompanied by the *tāra* (om) and others, consists of seventeen syllables:
*Tāraṃ namo bhagavate rāṃ ṅentaṃ mahā*. (62)
The mantra "puruṣāya padam" ending with "hṛt" consists of eighteen syllables;
Viśvāmitra is the sage, the Gāyatrī is the meter, and He Himself is the deity. (63)
That nineteen-syllable mantra, accompanied by the word "Kāma" and others, should be recited as follows: the syllable Om (Tāra), then the name, followed by the words "Bhagavate Rāmāya."
Having uttered the word "sarva," one should say "dehi me saubhāgyam";
then, having likewise uttered the wife of Vahni (svāhā), this mantra is considered to consist of twenty syllables.
One should utter "Tāraṃ namo bhagavate rāmāya sakalam" (Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed Lord Rāma, the whole [mantra]),
and then one should utter "āpannivāraṇāya svāhā" (for the warding off of calamities, the wife of Vahni).
The twenty-one-syllable mantra bestows all desired fruits: first the *tāra* (om), then *ramā* (śrīṃ), then one's own seed-syllable, and then *dāśarathāya*. (67)
Then one should utter the word "sarvābhīṣṭapadam" (the state of all desired things) for the beloved of Sītā;
then follows "dāya hṛt"; this mantra consists of twenty-two syllables.
One should utter the Tara (Om), then "Namo bhagavate vīrarāmāya," followed by "kala śatrūn hana dvandvam," and then say "vahnijāyā" (Svāhā). || 69 ||
The mantra consisting of twenty-three syllables is the destroyer of all enemies;
Viśvāmitra is declared to be the sage (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas). || 70 ||
The deity is this Vīrarāma; the seed-syllables and other elements are considered as before.
Having performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) according to the divisions of the root mantra, the wise practitioner [should proceed].
Having meditated upon Rāma, who stands with an arrow fixed to his bow, facing Rāvaṇa, mounted on his chariot, and holding the thunderbolt in his hand, one should recite the mantra.
One should utter the syllable *tāram*, then "namo bhagavate śrīrāmāya," and after saying "tārakabrahmaṇe," one should utter the words "māṃ tāraya. (73)
The mantra consisting of the essence of Tārā has twenty-four syllables;
one should perform everything, beginning with the seed-syllable, as previously described, just as in the case of the six-syllable mantra.
One should utter *kāma*, *tāra*, and *nati*, followed by the word *bhagavate*; then, having pronounced *rāmacandrāya*, one should speak the word *sakala*. (75)
"Janavaśyakarāya svāhā"—this mantra, consisting of twenty-five syllables, has desire as its essence and brings all under control. || 76 ||
The mantra joined with the *tāra* at the beginning consists of twenty-six syllables;
likewise, when joined with the *tāra* at the end, it consists of twenty-seven phonemes. || 77 ||
Tāraṃ namo bhagavate rakṣoghnaviśadāya ca | Having uttered "sarvavighnān," [one should recite] the two-word phrase "nivāraya. || 78 ||
This king of mantras ends with *svāhā* and consists of twenty-eight syllables; when joined with the *tāra* at the end, it consists of twenty-nine syllables. (79)
In the beginning, the mantra consists of thirty syllables conjoined with its own seed-syllable;
at the end as well, it is conjoined with that same [seed], and is thus remembered as consisting of thirty-one syllables.
O Rāmabhadra, O wielder of the great bow, O hero of the Raghus, O best of kings! O destroyer of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, grant us prosperity; give it to me! (81)
The seer is Anuṣṭubha Rāma, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is [Anuṣṭubh].
"Rāṃ" is its seed-syllable and "Yaṃ" is its power; one should employ it for the sake of one's desired object. (82)
Having placed one foot upon the heart, one should place the other foot upon the head;
having performed the nyāsa on the crest with five [syllables], one should perform the armor-nyāsa (kavaca) with three syllables.
One should cause the weapon-mantra to be bestowed with five colors upon the two eyes;
it is described as dark-complexioned, holding a bow and arrows, and accompanied by Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa. (84)
Having meditated upon Rāmacandra in one's heart— He who has come after slaying Rāvaṇa and has brought protection to the three worlds— one should recite the mantra one million times.
One should say "to the son of Daśaratha," then the word "vidmahe," then utter the word "Sītā," and then say "to the beloved. (86)
One should say "dhīmahi" and "tanno rāmaś cāpi pracodayāt";
this Gāyatrī, beginning with the syllable Om (Tārā), bestows liberation itself. || 87 ||
Even though Māyā and others possess wickedness, and Rāma and others are the abode of prosperity,
he, though joined with Madana, deludes the entire earth.
One should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) with five, three, and six syllables; with three and four syllables; and with four and four syllables. || 89 ||
One should perform all [rites], beginning with the seed-meditation (*bījadhyāna*), in sequence according to the six syllables:
*Tāraṃ*, *namo bhagavate*, and [the name] Raghunandana in the dative case. (90)
Then one should say "rakṣoghnaviśadaṃ tadvanmadhura" (pure like that which destroys demons and sweet), and thereafter,
with a serene countenance, one should say "amitatejase" ending in the suffix -ṅe.
The two forms of Balarāma ending in the dative case (caturthyanta), Viṣṇu ending in the accusative (ṅe-anta), and then the word "namas"—
this is declared to be the garland-mantra (mālāmanu) consisting of forty-seven syllables.
The seer, meter, deity, and so forth are Brahmā, Anuṣṭubh, and Rāghava;
the six limbs [of the mantra] are formed by the numbers seven, seven, seventeen, and six, corresponding to the seasons, the Saptadaśa-stoma, the Rudras, and the [six] seasons.
Meditation is declared to consist of ten syllables; one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
"Śriyai Sītāyai Svāhā"—this is the six-syllabled mantra ending in *svāhā* with the [dative] fourth case. (94)
Janaka is its seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is its meter (chandas), and the deity is Manu;
the blessed Sītā is said to be the mantra, with "Śrīṃ" as the seed-syllable and "Nati" as the power (śakti). || 95 ||
One should employ the *kīla* and *sītā* mantras ending in the fourth case for the desired purpose;
one should fashion the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by prefixing them with the long vowels.
One should meditate upon her who has a golden luster, whose hands hold a lotus, who is intent on gazing at Rāma, and who is adorned while seated upon the lap of Rāma in the center of a hexagon. 97.
Having extracted the syllable *la*, followed by "namo lakṣmaṇāya," Agastya is said to be its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Gāyatrī is its meter (*chanda*). || 98 ||

Lakṣmaṇa is declared to be the deity; "laṃ" is his seed-syllable (bīja), and indeed "namas" is his power (śakti); his application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha). || 99 ||
One should fashion the six limbs with one's own seed-syllable accompanied by the long vowel;
[the deity is] two-armed, with a body radiant like gold and eyes resembling lotuses. 100.
Having extracted the syllable *bha*, one should worship the God who holds a bow and arrows and is intent on the propitiation of Rāma, with the mantra "Bharatāya namaḥ" (Salutation to Bharata). 101.
The seer for this [mantra] is Agastya; then one should perform the remainder as before.
[One should meditate on] Bharata, who is dark-complexioned, peaceful, and devoted to the service of Rāma. (102)
I worship the hero, the son of Kaikeyī, who bears the bow and arrows;
having extracted the seed-syllable "Śam," [the mantra] ends with "Obeisance to Śatrughna.
As before, the seers and other elements are as follows, and its application is for the subduing of enemies.
I worship the son of Sumitrā, who has two arms, who possesses a golden luster, who is devoted to the service of Rāma, and who is the slayer of the demon Lavaṇa. 104.
"Hṛṃ Hanumān" ending in the dative case, followed by "hṛt," is the king of mantras;
Rāmacandra is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi); one should employ it according to the sequence as before. || 105 ||

"One should meditate upon me as a servant of Rāma, having two arms, possessing a golden luster, devoted solely to the service of Rāma, and equipped with a girdle of muñja grass and a loincloth. Thus [ends verse 106].
Thus ends the second chapter in the Ramarahasyopaniṣad. || 2 ||
The sages, Sanaka and the others, questioned Hanumān:
"O mighty son of Añjanā, please describe the worship altar (pūjā-pīṭha) for the mantras previously mentioned. Hanumān replied:
First, a hexagon; in its center, the seed-syllable of Rāma together with Śrī;

below that, the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the accusative case; above the seed-syllable, the name of the practitioner (sādhaka) in the genitive case; and on the sides, the seed-syllable of sight (dṛṣṭi), surrounding it.

The seed-syllables for subduing the vital force (*jīva*) and the power of breath (*prāṇa-śakti*) are as follows: all of these are encircled by two *praṇavas* facing each other. In the six corners—namely, the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, front, and back—they are endowed with the long vowels. The mantras beginning with the Heart mantra are to be placed in sequence.

[Rāṃ rīṃ rūṃ raiṃ rauṃ raḥ]—thus [the six long vowels] joined with that [syllable], ending with the weapon-mantra (astra) preceded by the heart (hṛdaya) and so forth; on the sides of the hexagon are the seed-syllables of Ramā and Māyā; at the tips of the corners is the Vārāha [syllable] "huṃ";
between those seed-syllables is the Kāma-bīja; all around is the Vāgbhava [syllable]; then three circles.
It has eight petals. On those petals, one should place the vowels and the eight groups of consonants; on each petal, six syllables of the *mālā-mantra*, and at the end, the five-syllable mantra.
On the flanks of those petals, one should place eight syllables. Then, there is another eight-petaled lotus.

On those petals is the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa; on the flanks of those petals is the seed-syllable of Śrī. Beyond that is a circle. Beyond that is a twelve-petaled lotus; on those petals is the twelve-syllabled mantra of Vāsudeva; on the flanks of those petals are the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.

Then the square; then the sixteen-petaled lotus. On those petals is the twelve-syllable mantra of Rāma accompanied by *huṃ* and *phaṭ*. On the edges of those petals is the *māyā*-seed syllable (*hrīṃ*).
Everywhere, on each edge, it is repeated twice: *hraṃ sraṃ bhraṃ braṃ bhramaṃ śruṃ*.
Then the *vṛtta* [square]. Then a lotus with thirty-two petals.
Within those petals is the *anuṣṭubh* mantra of the King of Mantras, Nṛsiṃha.
On the flanks of those petals are the mantras of the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, and the twelve Ādityas, beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
[The syllables] ending in the dative case follow in sequence. Outside of that, [the syllable] *vaṣaṭ* surrounds [it].

Then there is the *bhūpura* (fortress-city) joined with three lines. It is adorned with the zodiac signs and so forth in the twelve directions and presided over by the eight *nāgas*. In the four cardinal directions are the seed-syllables of Nṛsiṃha.

In the intermediate directions (vidikṣu) is the seed-syllable of Varāha. This entire yantra bestows all desires and grants liberation. This yantra pertains to [mantras] from one syllable up to nine syllables. It consists of ten enclosures (āvaraṇas). In the center of the hexagon...
One should worship Rāghava along with his limbs (*aṅga*). The first enclosure consists of the limbs in the six corners. At the base of the eight petals is the enclosure beginning with Ātman;
at their tips is the enclosure beginning with Vāsudeva. At the base of the second set of eight petals...
The first enclosure consists of Ghaṛṣṭi and others. In front of that is the enclosure of Hanumān and others.
On the twelve petals is the enclosure of Vasiṣṭha and others. On the sixteen petals is the enclosure of Nīla and others. On the thirty-two petals is the enclosure of Dhruva and others.
Within the perimeter of the earth-mandala is the enclosure of Indra and the other [guardians]; outside of that is the enclosure of the vajras and so forth.
Having worshipped in this manner, one should recite the mantra.
Now, the worship pedestal (*pūjāpīṭha*) for mantras consisting of ten to thirty-two syllables is described. First, a hexagon; in its center, one's own seed-syllable (*bīja*);
in its center, the names of those to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Thus, it is encircled by the *kāmabīja*. That—

The enclosure is performed with the remaining nine syllables. The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are placed in the six corners—at the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, east, and west. On its sides are *Śrī* and *Māyā*; at the tips of the corners is *Krodha*. Then follows a circle.

Then there is an eight-petalled lotus. On those petals, one should place the letters of the *mālā-mantra* in groups of six. On the flanks of those petals, one places the sixteen vowels. Then there is a circle. Surrounding that is the alphabet from *a* to *kṣa*. Outside of that is a *bhūpura* (fortress).
It has eight spokes at its tips; in the cardinal and intermediate directions are the forms of Narasiṃha and Vārāha.
This is the great yantra. It is the Vaiṣṇava pedestal beginning with Ādhāraśakti.
The first enclosure consists of the limbs [of the deity]. In the center is Rāma; on the left side...
[Sītā] in front of that, [Śārṅga bow and arrow]. At the base of the eight petals is the second enclosure, beginning with Hanumān and others. The third enclosure begins with Ghṛṣṭi and others.
The fourth is with Indra and others; the fifth is with the Vajra and other weapons. This is the propitiation of the yantra.
One should first recite the mantra consisting of ten syllables and so forth.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Rāmarahasyopaniṣad. || 3 ||
The sages, Sanaka and the others, questioned Hanumān:
"Please explain the procedure for the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) of the mantras of Śrī Rāma.
Hanumān replied:
Constantly bathing at the three periods of the day, subsisting on milk, roots, fruits, and the like;
or else, consuming only milk-rice (pāyasa) or sacrificial food (haviṣya). || 1 ||
Abandoning the six flavors and practicing the rules prescribed for his own stage of life,
he was pure and free from longing for women and other objects through speech, action, and mind.
Sleeping on the ground, practicing celibacy, free from desire, and devoted to his guru;
he was intent upon bathing, worship, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and libations.
Meditating on Rāma with undivided attention according to the path taught by the guru,
[one should practice] near the sun, the moon, Jupiter, a lamp, and so forth, as well as near cows and Brahmins.
In the presence of Śrī Rāma, remaining silent and contemplating the meaning of the mantra,
he sat upon a tiger-skin seat, following the sequence of postures such as the svastika.
At a place such as the root of a Tulasī, Pārijāta, or Śrīvṛkṣa tree,
[one should worship] with a rosary made of lotus seeds, Tulasī wood, or Rudrākṣa beads.
The practitioner of mantra, having worshipped upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal, should recite the mantra mentally with the Mātṛkā-mālā; he should perform one hundred thousand recitations of the syllables.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with milk-rice (pāyasa) using one-tenth of that amount;
from one-tenth of that, one should offer oblations (homa) with cow-ghee; and from one-tenth of that, one should feed [the Brahmins].
Then, one should perform the offering of a handful of flowers according to the rules with the root mantra.
Thereafter, having become one whose mantra is perfected, the sage shall be liberated while living.
The powers such as *aṇimā* attend upon him, just as a beautiful bride attends a young man,
both in worldly affairs and always during great calamities.
The Rāma-mantra should not be employed at all [for worldly ends], as it is solely the means for achieving liberation;
however, when worldly needs arise, one should remember me, the servant of Rāma.
O lords of sages, for that person who constantly remembers Rāma with devotion and is devoted to the Manu-mantra, I am consecrated for the attainment of his desired goal.
I shall grant the desired object to the devotees of Rāghava;
I am ever vigilant, bearing the full responsibility for Rāma’s work.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Rāmarahasyopaniṣad. || 4 ||
The sages, Sanaka and others, questioned Hanumān: "Please explain the meaning of the Śrī Rāma mantra. Hanumān replied:
"Among all the Rāma mantras, the six-syllabled one is the king of mantras."
In one way, in two ways, in three ways, in four ways, and likewise in five ways. || 1 ||
This [mantra] is established in six, seven, eight, and indeed many ways;
Śiva alone knows the greatness of the six-syllabled [mantra] according to its true nature. || 2 ||
This is declared to be the correct meaning of the King of Mantras, Śrī Rāma.
It applies likewise to the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa and the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva;
it consists of two meaningful syllables, "Rāma," wherein yogis take delight.
The syllable *ra* denotes fire and results in illumination. || 3 ||
The Supreme Self (Paramātman) is said to be its ultimate meaning, whose nature is Truth, Consciousness, and Bliss;
the consonant is the partless Brahman, while the vowel is the vital breath (prāṇa) and Māyā. || 4 ||
Know that the conjunction of vowels with consonants is the application of their vital breath;
therefore, the letter *ra* is joined to the *ā* and *ka* within the luminous [syllable].
The letter *ma* is proclaimed as *māyā* because it signifies manifestation;
since this is its own seed-syllable, it is called the Brahman of *samāya*.
That Puruṣa, together with the Bindu, possesses the nature of Śiva, Sūrya, and Indu;
his form is the Flame (Jyotis), and Nāda is considered to be Prakṛti along with him.
Both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are traditionally held to have arisen from Brahmā;
[he is] the seed consisting of Bindu and Nāda, and composed of the digits of Fire and Moon.
The form consisting of Agni and Soma is established within the seed-syllable of Rāma,
just as the primordial great tree resides within the seed of a banyan.
In the very same way, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings resides within the seed-syllable *rāma*;
the dual significance expressed by the seed-syllable is likewise seen in the name *Rāma*.
The seed-syllable free from illusion is proclaimed as the Supreme Brahman;
it grants liberation to practitioners, and thus the letter *Ma* is considered the bestower of liberation. (11)
Therefore, because he has the nature of Māra, Rāma bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
the letter *ra* is the meaning of the *tat-pada*, while the crocodile (*makara*) possesses the meaning of the *tvam-pada*.

The knowers of reality understand that the meaning of "asi" (art) is the union of those two; "namaḥ" (salutation) is to be understood as the meaning of "tvam" (you), and Rāma is said to be the meaning of "tat" (that). (13)
The dative case should be used in the sense of "for the sake of" (asīti-arthe); one should apply this principle to the mantras.
However, the statement "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and others grant liberation alone. || 14 ||
This bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; therefore, it excels even that [other means].
Among all these human beings, embodied souls possess the qualification for this. || 15 ||
He is always to be meditated upon as the *praṇava* by those seeking liberation, by the dispassionate, and by those dwelling in the stages of life (*āśrama*), especially by ascetics (*yati*).
One who understands the meaning of the Rāma-mantra is undoubtedly liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). || 16 ||
Whoever studies this Upaniṣad becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind; he becomes purified from the drinking of liquor;
he becomes purified from the theft of gold; he becomes purified from the murder of a Brahmin.
Having performed the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*) for the mantras of Rāma, he becomes Rāmacandra. This very point is expressed by a *ṛc*:
"Those who truly declare, 'I am always Rāma,' [attain liberation]."
They are certainly not worldly beings; they are surely Rāma himself, without a doubt.

Oṃ. That which is Ayodhyā is the foundational support (mūlādhārā) of all Vaikuṇṭhas; it is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of the Reality that is Brahman, stainless, supreme, and enriched with celestial jewel-treasures. Within it, there exists an eternally present place for the divine play of Śrī Sītā and Rāma.
Om. "Truth," thus [ends] the Upaniṣad.
Oṃ! O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious.
With steady limbs and bodies, may we praise you and attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the venerable Ramarahasyopaniṣad.
